mechanics.premise: A proud Igbo wrestling champion and warrior strives fiercely for status, but his fear of weakness and colonial disruption destroy him and his community.
mechanics.reader_promise: Authentic, dignified tragic epic portraying pre-colonial African society with internal complexity before British colonial-missionary disruption.
mechanics.opening: 'Okonkwo was well known throughout the nine villages and even beyond.' Establishes prowess through defeating Amalinze the Cat.
mechanics.point_of_view: Third-person communal voice incorporating Igbo oral storytelling cadences and idioms.
mechanics.character_system: Okonkwo (tragic hero), Unoka (flute-playing father foil), Nwoye (alienated son), Obierika (thoughtful philosopher friend), District Commissioner (colonial bureaucrat).
mechanics.conflict_and_stakes: Traditional clan cohesion and personal honor versus imperial colonial subjugation and internal cultural faultlines.
mechanics.structure: Three-part tripartite tragedy: Part 1 (rich Igbo society), Part 2 (exile in Mbanta), Part 3 (return and colonial collapse).
mechanics.scene_movement: Umuofia compound, wrestling arena, oracle cave, exile village of Mbanta, colonial church and court.
mechanics.dialogue: Richly ornamented with Igbo proverbs ('proverbs are the palm-oil with which words are eaten').
mechanics.setting: Umuofia and surrounding Igbo villages in late 19th-century Nigeria.
mechanics.style_and_devices: Oral vernacular integration in English, tragic hamartia, proverb rhetoric, objective historical realism.
mechanics.emotional_progression: Triumphant martial ascent -> brittle rigidity -> tragic exile -> desperate resistance -> solitary despair.
mechanics.suspense_or_anticipation: Okonkwo's extreme hyper-masculinity repeatedly collides with clan taboos (Peace Week beating, killing Ikemefuna).
mechanics.climax: Okonkwo decapitates the colonial court messenger at clan meeting, realizes with horror that his people will not go to war.
mechanics.ending: Okonkwo hangs himself; District Commissioner coldly decides to give him 'almost a whole paragraph' in his colonial book.
mechanics.conventions: Aristotelian tragic arc fused seamlessly with African communal storytelling and oral poetics.
mechanics.innovation_or_subversion: Directly refutes colonial literature (such as Joyce Cary's *Mister Johnson*) by restoring sovereign African narrative voice.
mechanics.critical_reception: Landmark cornerstone of modern African literature; translated into over 50 languages.
mechanics.audience_reception: Globally revered masterpiece reshaping post-colonial world literature and education.
